item.title: 4 Questions for When You Don't Know What to Do Next
item.description:
Decision-Making

4 Questions for When You Don't Know What to Do Next

How to expand your perspective and find a way forward when you feel stuck.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • A quick internal check-in can help us notice what we already know.
  • A four-step practice can help us widen our perspective when we feel stuck.
  • One small next step can help us begin moving forward differently.

There are moments in life when we know something needs to change, but we may not be sure of what to do next.

Maybe a decision feels complicated, a pattern we've been repeating is no longer working, or we just feel a little... stuck.

When we're in one of these moments, it can be tempting to immediately look outside ourselves for an answer. We ask other people what they think, search for advice, or spend even more time thinking things through, but from only one angle. Sometimes, before we look outside ourselves, it can help to pause and check in with what we already know.

3 Check-Ins to Know If Something Is Right for You

When you are wondering if something is a fit for you, consulting what you already know before going to look for outside answers can be a good place to start. There are three places worth checking in with, or three questions I like to ask:

  1. How does this feel in my nervous system? I don’t just mean in the moment you’re asking yourself. Pay attention to how your body feels when you’re in the situation, or when you imagine yourself making the decision, saying yes or saying no, staying, leaving, continuing, or changing course. Excitement, tension, dread, and even relief are all information.
  2. What do my instincts say? Underneath the noise, most of us have a steadier inner knowing. Some may call it a gut feeling or intuition. Maybe you think about it as your "spidey senses." It’s the part of us that recognizes our excuses or when we’re telling ourselves a story that doesn’t quite hold true. The idea here is to notice what your initial, unfiltered response was, before you talked yourself into or out of it.
  3. How does this align with my values? Sometimes the choices that align most deeply with our values are the ones that ask us to stretch, take a risk, or step outside what’s comfortable. This can be especially true when we’re trying to make a change that matters, maybe not just to ourselves but also to the people around us. When a decision aligns with your values, it can still feel hard, but it tends to feel manageable, even in the discomfort.

Sometimes this self-check can bring a clear answer right away. Other times, especially when a situation is layered, long-standing, or particularly sticky, it can help to slow down further and widen the lens.

The 4-Step Perspective Practice

A framework I turn to often in coaching and in my own life to help make sense of sticky situations, solve problems, and figure out what to do next involves looking back, looking in, looking around, and looking ahead.

Each question invites us to see something we might miss when we're looking at a situation from only one angle.

  • Look back. What does this situation have to teach me? What can I learn from what has happened?
  • Look in. What is this revealing about myself? What am I feeling, needing, or noticing?
  • Look around. How is this affecting the people around me?
  • Look ahead. What's one small step I can take to move forward differently?

This framework gives us a way to expand our perspective without judging ourselves for where we are.

Let's say you've noticed that you've been stuck in people-pleasing patterns. You've been saying yes when you really want to say no, overextending yourself for other people, or putting everyone else's needs ahead of your own. Here's what this might look like in practice:

  • Looking back: The reality is that every behaviour served a purpose at some point. If you're tired of overextending yourself for other people, it's worth asking how that pattern once helped you. Maybe it kept you safe or helped you keep the peace.
  • Looking in: This is where we notice what we're wanting, what we're needing, and what's actually true for us right now, underneath the guilt or the shame that so often shows up. Maybe you're feeling weary or perhaps fed up. Maybe you're finally ready for something to shift.
  • Looking around: This can help us see the situation a little differently. If you've been pouring your energy into everyone else's needs, chances are it is not only costing you but also the people who matter most to you, when they end up with whatever is left over at the end of the day.
  • Looking ahead: Perhaps it's recognizing the importance of protecting your well-being and caring for yourself as part of your home team. One small step is enough to start making a change. If the goal is learning to hold a boundary, you might try saying no to something small and manageable before you try it in a higher-stakes relationship or situation.

My gentle invitation for you is to think of a recurring challenge or situation in your life that feels a little sticky.

What can you learn by looking back?

What are you noticing when you look in?

What becomes clearer when you look around?

And what might be possible when you look ahead?

A wider lens can help us notice what we couldn't see before, understand what we need, and find a next step that feels a little more possible.

Final Thoughts

Deep down, we often already know the next right step. What makes it hard is that it requires us to move beyond what's familiar or do something we haven't done before. It requires us to trust ourselves enough to take the step, even when it's hard.

If you're navigating a sticky situation or faced with a hard decision right now, try checking in with your body, noticing what your intuition is already telling you, and asking whether it aligns with what matters most to you. And if you need more, widen the lens by looking back, looking in, looking around, and looking ahead.

Sometimes, the clarity we're looking for comes when we give ourselves the chance to slow down, really check in with ourselves, and see things differently.

item.title: Why Universities Keep Lowering Their Standards
item.description:
Education

Why Universities Keep Lowering Their Standards

Declining college standards: Less about villains, more about incentives.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Declining university standards are less about bloated administrators or lazy faculty than bad incentives.
  • Enrollment and funding pressures push universities to lower admissions and grading standards.
  • Faculty rationally inflate grades and reduce work due to student evaluations and career incentives.
  • Realigning incentives, not moral appeals or denunciations, is needed to restore academic rigor.
Source: Gemini AI image/Free Use

Higher education has seen better days. The recent high-profile case of plagiarism and dishonesty by former Cambridge professor Jason Arday has become a flashpoint in a broader debate over whether universities still maintain the academic excellence they claim to value. Many on the political right argue that the left-wing ideology that elevated Arday is eroding traditional standards. Liberal critics tell a different story, blaming corporatization and a consumer model that treats students as customers. The rise of adjunct instruction and decline of tenure-track positions, they argue, have further eroded expectations and professionalism. Both sides nevertheless converge on a diagnosis: rampant grade inflation and declining academic rigor are chipping away at public trust in what a college degree actually signals.

What is often missing from this debate is the question of incentives. Charlie Munger, the longtime vice chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, was famous for insisting on their decisive power. “Show me the incentive,” he liked to say, “and I’ll show you the outcome.”

One of his favorite examples involved FedEx. Its overnight system depended on workers unloading, sorting, and reloading packages at a central hub with almost no margin for delay. Yet planes kept leaving late. Managers’ efforts to encourage teamwork barely moved productivity. The fix was simple: Pay workers by the shift rather than by the hour. Once the planes were loaded, they could go home. The delays vanished. Paying by the hour had been a perverse incentive—workers had nothing to gain from moving faster.

Higher Ed’s Perverse Incentives Have No Quick Fix

Higher education is more complicated. Universities are not merely delivering a product; they are expected to cultivate citizens capable of participating in democratic life and contributing to the economy. That requires rigorous standards that equip graduates to navigate serious challenges, from AI disruption to unsustainable debt and ecological uncertainties.

Regrettably, the most powerful incentives facing higher education work against those standards.

Consider enrollment pressures. Although elite institutions and flagship state universities remain comparatively insulated, the pressure to attract and retain students is intensifying across the sector. The impending enrollment cliff creates a direct incentive for tuition-dependent universities to lower admissions standards simply to fill seats. State reimbursement formulas tied to graduation numbers compound the problem, pushing institutions toward looser degree requirements or grade inflation to boost completion rates.

It is unsurprising, then, that roughly 90 percent of U.S. universities are now test-optional or test-free. Raising the admissions bar threatens enrollment and fiscal health. Equally unsurprising is the growth in student-support infrastructure—advising, counseling, tutoring, and mental-health services. The more underprepared students an institution admits, the greater the pressure to help them persist to graduation.

And underprepared they are. Recent NAEP data show a troubling deterioration in academic achievement, particularly in reading, with 12th-grade scores falling to their lowest level in decades. Recent ACT data tell a similar story: average scores have declined substantially since the mid-1990s. Yet high school grades continue to rise.

The result is a troubling disconnect: Students’ measured competencies appear to be declining while their grades signal the opposite. The same pattern is evident in higher education. A’s and B’s now constitute the overwhelming majority of grades at many colleges, while D’s and F’s have become vanishingly rare. There are even calls to abolish grades altogether. Western Oregon University recently eliminated D− and F grades for undergraduates, while the University of Michigan will replace first-semester letter grades with “Pass” or “No Credit” beginning in 2027.

Less About Villains, More About Incentives

It is easy to malign such decisions as short-sighted or corrupt. Conservative critics often treat changing grading policies and "administrative bloat" as bad choices driven by overemphasis on equity and mental health at the expense of competence and grit. Yet as students arrive less prepared, an administrator's primary responsibility is protecting the institution's fiscal health. Debates over higher education too often ignore the constraints shaping stakeholders' behavior.

Faculty are no exception. It is easy to criticize them for abandoning rigorous instruction. Yet given the incentives they face, their decisions to inflate grades and reduce coursework are predictable.

Student teaching evaluations are central to the story. Course ease has been shown to be a leading predictor of high student evaluations. Probationary faculty seeking tenure—and adjuncts hoping to keep their contracts—have compelling reasons not to antagonize students who influence their career prospects. Add a traditional reward system that prioritizes research productivity, and the question is clear: Why would professors risk student and administrative pushback by insisting on high standards?

The result is a system in which nearly every actor—administrators, admissions officers, and faculty—faces incentives that pull against rigor. Munger never suggested FedEx simply needed better employees. He understood that people respond to the incentives in front of them. Until those incentives are redesigned, no amount of ideological critique, from the right or the left, will restore the rigor of the college degree.

A Much-Needed Conversation About Incentives

I cannot pretend to have a magic-bullet solution to this structural problem. My colleagues and I argue that a renewed national commitment to both public financing of higher education and high academic standards is overdue. At present, we have the opposite: a student-debt-financed system encouraging ever-greater enrollment while weakening the signals that tell us what students can actually do. We are producing more graduates with high grades but, too often, insufficient marketable skills while student debt approaches $2 trillion.

From a post-tribal perspective, liberals have to take seriously the conservative argument that not everyone is suited for a four-year college degree. Conservatives, in turn, have to acknowledge that access to higher education should not depend on family wealth. Greater public financing, combined with meaningful admissions and learning standards, may offer a better path forward.

The alternative is to keep passing underprepared students from high school and through college with massive debt and unverified skills. It's easier in the short term to kick the can. But what happens when the diploma no longer signals competence?

Bad incentives can explain how we got here. They can't excuse where we go next.

item.title: Why People Disappoint Us in Relationships
item.description:
Relationships

Why People Disappoint Us in Relationships

When someone disappoints us, it may not mean they don’t care.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • When someone disappoints us repeatedly, it does not always mean they care less than we do.
  • People tend to put in the amount of effort that a relationship has come to require.
  • Raising the bar works best when expectations are clear, specific, respectful, and introduced one at a time.

A common assumption about long-term relationships, both romantic relationships and friendships, is that if the other person truly cares about us, they will demonstrate it by generally being thoughtful, considerate, appreciative of the efforts we make, and willing to make similar efforts themselves. If their efforts keep disappointing us, we believe it is because they do not care about us as much as we do about them.

But that assumption is often incorrect.

One of the realities of human psychology is that most people rise only to the bar that was set for them. If the bar was set too low, few people will voluntarily exceed it, because we naturally seek to conserve mental and emotional energy. Psychologists sometimes describe people as “cognitive misers,” meaning we tend to look for ways to accomplish our goals while expending the least possible mental effort.

Decades of research support this idea. When people can choose between two tasks that produce the same outcome—but one requires more mental effort—they will consistently choose the less demanding option.

People allocate their effort where and when it seems most necessary. And in relationships, what seems necessary is usually defined by the expectations that have been set—by you.

Ask yourself, Have I unintentionally set the bar too low? When my partner disappoints me, do I let them know that clearly, or make excuses for them? Do I constantly initiate contact with a friend but never address it when they don’t? Do I rarely ask for support? Do I tolerate poor communication or inconsiderate behavior without pushing back?

If you can answer yes to any of these questions, you might have set the bar too low. And if so, then the other person is simply operating at the level of effort that you established for them.

How to Raise Expectations Without Blowing Up a Relationship

Low bars can be reset but you need to do so thoughtfully. Changing a longstanding dynamic in a relationship is like turning a large ship: it takes time and steady effort to adjust course.

Step 1: Identify the Real Issues

Choose the issues that truly matter and that affect the health of the relationship, and address those—for example, lack of communication, unequal emotional support, imbalance in responsibilities, or lack of consideration.

Step 2: Raise One Issue at a Time

This is crucial. If you raise five issues at once, the other person will feel overwhelmed and criticized. Instead, pick one to address first. Changing one behavior at a time is more realistic and more likely to succeed.

Step 3: Turn Silent Expectations into Clear Requests

Do not assume the other person should “just know” what you need. Express your expectations clearly—not as accusations, but as requests. Requests raise the bar without triggering defensiveness. Instead of saying, "You never check in with me," you could say, "It would mean a lot to me if you checked in with me once during the workday."

Step 4: Reinforce the Expectation

If the behavior doesn’t change immediately, don’t assume your conversation failed. You’re asking the person to invest more energy than they have been investing. That adjustment takes time and repetition. Reinforce the expectation kindly and respectfully. For example, "Remember when we talked about checking in during the workday? I’d really appreciate it if you could make that a daily habit."

Step 5: Be Patient

Relationships have momentum. If a pattern has existed for years, it won’t reverse overnight. Consistent, respectful adjustments gradually raise the bar. Lastly, when entering new relationships of any kind, pay attention to the expectations you’re setting, and set the bar where you want it to be from the start.

Adapted from my Substack newsletter The Psychology Lab

item.title: How Grief Affects a Dysfunctional Family
item.description:
Grief

How Grief Affects a Dysfunctional Family

Grief doesn’t create dysfunction. It magnifies patterns already there.

Posted August 13, 2026

Key points
  • Grief can magnify existing family dysfunction.
  • Loss can turn grief reactions into blame, aggression, or withdrawal.
  • Healthy grieving may require setting boundaries with difficult relatives.
Source: AI generated

Grief is difficult under the best of circumstances. The death of a loved one can bring sadness, anger, guilt, regret, confusion, and even relief. But in dysfunctional families, grief does not occur in isolation. It enters a family system where conflict, resentment, poor communication, unhealthy roles, and unresolved wounds may already exist.

In healthy families, grief can bring people together. Family members may comfort one another, share memories, divide responsibilities, and make space for different expressions of loss.

In emotionally unhealthy families, death can do the opposite. Rather than healing old wounds, grief may reopen them. Existing family dynamics can become more intense, and disagreements that once simmered beneath the surface may erupt.

Stages of Grief

You may be familiar with the Kübler-Ross framework1, which describes five experiences commonly associated with grief: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance.

These are not necessarily linear stages, nor does everyone experience all five. But they provide a useful framework for thinking about what can happen when grief collides with an already dysfunctional family system. In these families, grief may not simply bring difficult emotions to the surface. It can amplify existing patterns2,3.

The Altered Stages of Grief

Denial can become delusion. Death sometimes changes the family narrative overnight. A difficult or abusive relative may suddenly be remembered as nearly flawless. Painful experiences may be minimized, denied, or rewritten.

Family members may also exaggerate the closeness of their relationship with the deceased. Someone who was largely absent may suddenly present themselves as the person who knew them best. In some cases, idealizing the deceased—or overstating one's role in their life—may help protect against guilt, regret, or unresolved conflict.

Anger can become aggression. Grief often includes anger. But relatives who already struggle with emotional regulation may direct that anger toward everyone around them.

They may become hostile, provoke arguments, lash out at caregivers, or resurrect conflicts that have little to do with the death itself. Instead of grieving together, family members begin fighting one another.

Bargaining can become blame. After a death, people naturally ask questions: Could something have been done differently? What if we had noticed sooner? What if another decision had been made?

In dysfunctional families, those questions can turn into a search for someone to blame. The primary caregiver may become an easy target. Relatives who were minimally involved may suddenly scrutinize medical decisions, caregiving choices, or end-of-life decisions. Blame can provide a temporary sense of control over something that was ultimately painful and uncontrollable.

Depression can become disappearance. Some people cope with overwhelming emotions by withdrawing. Family members with limited coping skills may become emotionally unavailable, avoid funeral planning, stop communicating, or leave others to manage practical responsibilities. Their disappearance may be physical, emotional, or both.

Unfortunately, this often means that the family members who were already carrying the greatest burden before the death are left carrying the load afterward as well.

Acceptance can become accusation. There is no correct way to grieve, and there is no universal timeline. Yet dysfunctional families may create rules about what grief is supposed to look like. Someone who returns to work, laughs, travels, celebrates a birthday, or simply begins functioning again may be accused of being insensitive.

You moved on too quickly.

You don't seem sad enough.

You must not have really loved them.

Grief can become another opportunity for policing, judging, and controlling other family members.

Sometimes the opposite happens. A person who continues grieving may be criticized for being unable to “get over it.” Either way, the message is the same: You are grieving incorrectly.

Grieving in an Unhealthy Family

When the family system itself is contributing to your distress, protecting your emotional health may require grieving differently.

Focus on your own mourning. Family conflict can become a powerful distraction from grief. Arguments, accusations, funeral disputes, and old resentments can consume so much emotional energy that you never have space to process the loss itself. Pay attention to what you are feeling rather than becoming absorbed in everyone else's reactions.

Limit interactions with difficult relatives. You do not have to attend every gathering or participate in every family conversation. You might attend the funeral but skip the repast. You might leave an event early. In some circumstances, you may decide not to attend services at all and instead honor the deceased privately in a way that feels meaningful to you.

Lean into emotionally healthy people. Your strongest support may or may not come from relatives. Seek out friends, partners, extended family members, clergy, therapists, or others who can offer comfort without creating additional conflict.

Be mindful of numbing behavior. Alcohol, drugs, compulsive behaviors, and other forms of avoidance may temporarily dull painful emotions, but they do not resolve them. Healthy grief requires finding ways to experience and manage painful emotions rather than continually escaping them.

Remember...

Everyone in the family may be hurting. Their pain may help explain their behavior, but it does not give them unlimited permission to hurt you.

You can have compassion for another person's grief without absorbing their anger, accepting their accusations, or carrying their emotional burden.

You are allowed to grieve the person you lost without also becoming responsible for managing the family they left behind.
